key_findings.claim: Self-supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) features contain explicit information about the semantic segmentation of an image.
key_findings.evidence: This information does not emerge as clearly with supervised ViTs, nor with convolutional networks (convnets).

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised ViT features are excellent k-NN classifiers.
key_findings.evidence: Reaching 78.3% top-1 on ImageNet with a small ViT.

key_findings.claim: Momentum encoder, multi-crop training, and the use of small patches are important for ViTs.
key_findings.evidence: Our study also underlines the importance of momentum encoder [33], multi-crop training [10], and the use of small patches with ViTs.

key_findings.claim: DINO is a simple self-supervised method that can be interpreted as a form of self-distillation with no labels.
key_findings.evidence: We implement our ﬁndings into a simple self-supervised method, called DINO, which we interpret as a form of self-distillation with no labels.

key_findings.claim: There is a synergy between DINO and ViTs.
key_findings.evidence: Achieving 80.1% top-1 on ImageNet in linear evaluation with ViT-Base.

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised ViT features explicitly contain the scene layout and object boundaries.
key_findings.evidence: This information is directly accessible in the self-attention modules of the last block, as shown in Figure 1.

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised ViT features perform particularly well with a basic nearest neighbors classifier (k-NN).
key_findings.evidence: Achieving 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet without any finetuning, linear classifier, nor data augmentation.

key_findings.claim: The emergence of segmentation masks is a property shared across self-supervised methods.
key_findings.evidence: The good performance with k-NN only emerges when combining certain components such as momentum encoder [33] and multi-crop augmentation [10].

key_findings.claim: Using smaller patches with ViTs is important to improve the quality of the resulting features.
key_findings.evidence: Another ﬁnding from our study is the importance of using smaller patches with ViTs to improve the quality of the resulting features.

key_findings.claim: DINO can work with only a centering and sharpening of the teacher output to avoid collapse.
key_findings.evidence: Other popular components such as predictor [30], advanced normalization [10] or contrastive loss [33] add little beneﬁts in terms of stability or performance.

key_findings.claim: The DINO framework is flexible and works on both convnets and ViTs.
key_findings.evidence: Without the need to modify the architecture, nor adapt internal normalizations [58].

key_findings.claim: DINO works with convnets.
key_findings.evidence: Matching the state of the art with a ResNet-50 architecture.

key_findings.claim: Training DINO with ViT achieves 76.1% on ImageNet linear benchmark with significantly reduced compute requirements.
key_findings.evidence: Takes just two 8-GPU servers over 3 days, outperforming self-supervised systems based on convnets of comparable sizes [10, 30].

key_findings.claim: DINO completes the interpretation of self-supervised learning as a form of Mean Teacher self-distillation with no labels.
key_findings.evidence: Our approach takes its inspiration from BYOL but operates with a different similarity matching loss and uses the exact same architecture for the student and the teacher.
key_findings.limitations: Previous works rely on a pre-trained fixed teacher while DINO's teacher is dynamically built during training.

key_findings.claim: DINO extends knowledge distillation to the case where no labels are available.
key_findings.evidence: Our work builds on this relation and extends knowledge distillation to the case where no labels are available.

key_findings.claim: Freezing the teacher network over an epoch works surprisingly well in DINO.
key_findings.evidence: Copying the student weight for the teacher fails to converge.

key_findings.claim: Using an exponential moving average (EMA) on the student weights (momentum encoder) is particularly well suited for DINO.
key_findings.evidence: Of particular interest, using an exponential moving average (EMA) on the student weights, i.e., a momentum encoder [33], is particularly well suited for our framework.

key_findings.claim: The momentum teacher in DINO performs a form of model ensembling (Polyak-Ruppert averaging) and consistently outperforms the student during training.
key_findings.evidence: This teacher has better performance than the student throughout the training, guiding the student by providing higher quality target features. This dynamic was not observed in previous works [30, 58].

key_findings.claim: DINO does not use a predictor, resulting in the exact same architecture for both student and teacher networks.
key_findings.evidence: We do not use a predictor [30, 16], resulting in the exact same architecture in both student and teacher networks.

key_findings.claim: DINO applied to ViT is entirely Batch Normalization (BN)-free.
key_findings.evidence: ViT architectures do not use batch normalizations (BN) by default. Therefore, when applying DINO to ViT we do not use any BN also in the projection heads.

key_findings.claim: Centering and sharpening are complementary in avoiding collapse.
key_findings.evidence: Centering prevents one dimension to dominate but encourages collapse to the uniform distribution, while sharpening has the opposite effect. Applying both operations balances their effects, which is sufficient to avoid collapse in presence of a momentum teacher (Section 5.3).

key_findings.claim: The centering method to avoid collapse trades stability for less dependence over the batch.
key_findings.evidence: The centering operation only depends on ﬁrst-order batch statistics and can be interpreted as adding a bias term c to the teacher. The center c is updated with an exponential moving average, which allows the approach to work well across different batch sizes (Section 5.5).

key_findings.claim: DINO performs on par with the state of the art on ResNet-50.
key_findings.evidence: Validating that DINO works in the standard setting.

key_findings.claim: DINO outperforms BYOL, MoCov2, and SwAV when using a ViT architecture.
key_findings.evidence: DINO outperforms BYOL, MoCov2 and SwAV by +3.5% with linear classiﬁcation and by +7.9% with k-NN evaluation.

key_findings.claim: Performance with a simple k-NN classifier is almost on par with a linear classifier when using DINO with ViT architectures.
key_findings.evidence: 74.5% versus 77.0%. This property emerges only when using DINO with ViT architectures, and does not appear with other existing self-supervised methods nor with a ResNet-50.

key_findings.claim: Reducing the size of patches has a bigger impact on performance than training a larger ViT with DINO.
key_findings.evidence: While training a larger ViT with DINO improves the performance, reducing the size of the patches (“/8” variants) has a bigger impact on the performance.
key_findings.limitations: Reducing the patch size leads to a significant reduction of running time and larger memory usage.

key_findings.claim: A base ViT with 8x8 patches trained with DINO achieves 80.1% top-1 in linear classification and 77.4% with a k-NN classifier.
key_findings.evidence: This is achieved with 10x less parameters and 1.4x faster run time than previous state of the art [13].

key_findings.claim: DINO features outperform those trained on ImageNet with labels for image retrieval.
key_findings.evidence: Observed in Table 3.

key_findings.claim: DINO ViT features trained on GLDv2 are remarkably good for landmark retrieval.
key_findings.evidence: Outperforming previously published methods based on off-the-shelf descriptors [68, 57].

key_findings.claim: ViT trained with DINO is very competitive on copy detection.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 shows that ViT trained with DINO is very competitive on copy detection.

key_findings.claim: DINO's performance is competitive on video instance segmentation.
key_findings.evidence: Even though our training objective nor our architecture are designed for dense tasks, the performance is competitive on this benchmark (Table 5).

key_findings.claim: For dense recognition tasks, ViT variants with small patches perform much better.
key_findings.evidence: +9.1% (J &F)m for ViT-B with “/8” patches.

key_findings.claim: Different attention heads in DINO-trained ViT can attend to different semantic regions of an image.
key_findings.evidence: Even when they are occluded (the bushes on the third row) or small (the ﬂag on the second row), as shown in Fig. 3.

key_findings.claim: Supervised ViT does not attend well to objects in presence of clutter, unlike DINO models.
key_findings.evidence: A clear difference between the supervised or DINO models with a signiﬁcant gap in terms of Jaccard similarities is observed when probing self-attention maps (Fig. 4).
key_findings.limitations: The self-attention maps are smooth and not optimized to produce a mask.

key_findings.claim: For ViT architectures, self-supervised pretraining transfers better than features trained with supervision.
key_findings.evidence: This is consistent with observations made on convolutional networks [10, 33, 62].

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised pretraining greatly improves results on ImageNet.
key_findings.evidence: Results improve by +1-2%.

key_findings.claim: The momentum encoder is important for DINO's performance and to avoid collapse without advanced operations like SK.
key_findings.evidence: In the absence of momentum, our framework does not work (Table 7, row 2) and more advanced operations, SK for example, are required to avoid collapse (Table 7, row 9). With momentum, using SK has little impact (Table 7, row 3).

key_findings.claim: Multi-crop training and the cross-entropy loss in DINO are important components to obtain good features.
key_findings.evidence: Observed in rows 4 and 5 of Table 7.

key_findings.claim: Adding a predictor to the student network has little impact in DINO.
key_findings.evidence: It is critical in BYOL to prevent collapse [16, 30].

key_findings.claim: Performance greatly improves as patch size decreases.
key_findings.evidence: Observed in Fig. 5 for ViT-S models trained with different patch sizes (16x16, 8x8, 5x5).
key_findings.limitations: The performance gain from using smaller patches comes at the expense of throughput (e.g., 5x5 patches fall to 44 im/s, vs 180 im/s for 8x8 patches).

key_findings.claim: Using a teacher from the previous epoch does not collapse and provides competitive k-NN performance.
key_findings.evidence: Competitive with existing frameworks such as MoCo-v2 or BYOL. However, a momentum encoder clearly provides superior performance.

key_findings.claim: The momentum teacher in DINO constantly outperforms the student during training.
key_findings.evidence: This behavior has not been observed by other frameworks also using momentum [33, 30], nor when the teacher is built from the previous epoch.

key_findings.claim: Multi-crop training improves the accuracy/running-time tradeoff for DINO runs.
key_findings.evidence: The performance is 74.6% in 24 hours with 2x224^2+10x96^2 crop setting, while 72.5% after 46 hours of training without multi-crop (2x224^2).
key_findings.limitations: Memory usage is higher with multi-crop (15.4G versus 9.3G).

key_findings.claim: The performance boost from multi-crop (local-to-global augmentation) cannot be caught up by more training without it.
key_findings.evidence: The performance boost brought with multi-crop cannot be caught up by more training in the 2x224^2 setting, which shows the value of the “local-to-global” augmentation.

key_findings.claim: The gain from adding more views diminishes for longer trainings.
key_findings.evidence: +0.2% from 6x to 10x 96^2 crops.

key_findings.claim: Models can be trained to high performance with small batches using DINO.
key_findings.evidence: Table 9 confirms this. Results with batch size of 128 are slightly below default (1024).
key_findings.limitations: Results with smaller batch sizes (bs = 128) are slightly below our default training setup of bs = 1024, and would certainly require to re-tune hyperparameters like the momentum rates for example.

key_findings.claim: DINO shows potential for training large models that barely fit an image per GPU.
key_findings.evidence: Training a model with a batch size of 8 reached 35.2% after 50 epochs.

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised pretraining of a standard ViT model has potential, achieving performance comparable to the best convnets specifically designed for this setting.
key_findings.evidence: Achieving performance that are comparable with the best convnets speciﬁcally designed for this setting.

key_findings.claim: Two properties emerged from DINO-trained ViT features that can be leveraged in future applications: high quality k-NN features and scene layout information.
key_findings.evidence: The quality of the features in k-NN classiﬁcation has a potential for image retrieval where ViT are already showing promising results [22]. The presence of information about the scene layout in the features can also beneﬁt weakly supervised image segmentation.

key_findings.claim: Self-supervised learning could be the key to developing a BERT-like model based on ViT.
key_findings.evidence: We have evidences that self-supervised learning could be the key to developing a BERT-like model based on ViT.
